profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between a local authority disabled children's service manager and an NHS community child health pathway coordinator to finalize handoffs for a borough-wide expansion of a key worker service for disabled children. The service is moving from a small pilot to routine use across health, education, and social care after families reported that having one named coordinator reduced duplication and confusion. Agenda: confirm when a referral is treated as having entered the key worker pathway, align what information the shared plan should contain and where partners will look for it, agree what the monthly update will include for cross-agency visibility, and clarify what it means for the key worker team to 'own' the central tracker. Expected outcome: both participants leave believing they have settled the operational interface for caseload reporting, shared documentation, monthly status reporting, and tracker ownership ahead of the next intake wave.

members.name: Helen Morris
members.role: Local Authority Disabled Children's Service Manager
members.expertise: Integrated service delivery, family support pathways, early help operations, multi-agency coordination
members.background: Helen has worked in children's social care for 12 years and now oversees the borough's disability family support and early help coordination functions; she designed much of the original key worker pilot and works closely with schools, SEND caseworkers, and voluntary sector family support teams.
members.private_state: Helen wants the borough-wide rollout to feel simple for families and administratively light for her team, and she is especially concerned about avoiding duplicate requests for information and preventing the key worker role from turning into a reporting-heavy coordination hub.
hidden_assumptions: A child is 'active' in the key worker service once a named key worker is allocated and the family has accepted contact, because practical coordination begins at that point.
The 'shared plan' is the family-facing action summary generated from the local authority record and circulated as a PDF, even if fuller notes exist elsewhere.
If both sides agree the monthly update will include current action statuses, that means reporting only actions whose status has changed, slipped, or become risky since the last update.
If the key worker team 'owns' the tracker, that means her team is the single point of data entry and other agencies send amendments to them rather than editing directly.
When partners say they need visibility for governance, a concise exceptions-based summary is normally sufficient unless someone explicitly asks for a full return.

members.name: Dr. Amir Qureshi
members.role: NHS Community Child Health Pathway Coordinator
members.expertise: Community paediatrics operations, MDT workflow design, referral triage, SEND-linked health coordination
members.background: Amir is a clinician-manager who coordinates intake and operational flow across community paediatrics, therapy services, and multidisciplinary review meetings; before joining the trust he worked in an area where key worker functions sat inside a more formal MDT governance structure with shared templates and recurring case-status reporting.
members.private_state: Amir wants the expanded key worker service to fit cleanly into existing NHS governance expectations and is quietly worried that family-friendly informal coordination could leave health actions insufficiently documented or too dependent on one team's narrative summary.
hidden_assumptions: A child is only 'active' once the first documented multi-agency review has taken place and an agreed cross-agency plan is formally open, because only then is the case operationally live across services.
The 'shared plan' is the structured MDT template in the shared Teams workspace, with standard sections completed by each participating service before or after review.

If both sides agree the monthly update will include current action statuses, that means a complete line-by-line status for every open action on every active case, including actions that remain unchanged.
If the key worker team 'owns' the tracker, that means they host the file, maintain the structure, and chase contributors, while each agency still enters and updates its own rows directly.
For governance and assurance, 'current status' normally implies a full standing return rather than an exceptions-only note, unless someone explicitly narrows it.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of an 'active' key worker case
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to move referrals into the active caseload quickly and to use active case numbers in routine reporting.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Helen means a child becomes active as soon as a named key worker is allocated and the family accepts support.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Amir means a child becomes active only after the first documented multi-agency review opens the coordinated plan.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both thresholds are common and defensible in integrated services, and because the discussion is about keeping referrals moving rather than auditing the counting rule itself, the familiar term 'active' creates a strong false sense of alignment.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the shared plan should show current actions, owners, deadlines, and the latest family priorities before the next review cycle.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Helen is referring to the PDF family-facing action summary exported from the local authority case record and sent out as the practical working version.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Amir is referring to the structured MDT plan stored in the cross-agency Teams folder, with standard sections populated by different services.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The fields they discuss—actions, owners, deadlines, and family priorities—fit naturally on both artifacts, so the content agreement sounds like document alignment even though each person is picturing a different file.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for monthly updates to include 'current action statuses'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the monthly update will include current action statuses so partners can see what is still open and what has moved on.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Helen believes this requirement is satisfied by an exceptions-based summary listing only actions with a new status, slippage, escalation, or other meaningful change since the previous month.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Amir believes this requirement is satisfied only by a comprehensive monthly status return showing the current state of every open action, including those with no change.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because they explicitly agree on the contents using the same phrase—'current action statuses'—it sounds as though they have resolved the agenda item; the divergence sits in the unstated sufficiency criterion for what counts as including those statuses.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for the key worker team to 'own' the tracker
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the key worker team will own the central tracker so there is one clear home for cross-agency actions.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Helen interprets ownership as central administrative control: her team maintains the live entries, updates rows after family or partner contact, and receives amendments from other agencies by email or message.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Amir interprets ownership as stewardship of the shared artifact: the key worker team hosts the file, sets conventions, and chases completeness, but each agency updates its own actions directly in the tracker.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The agenda item appears settled because they use the explicit language of 'ownership,' but that word often bundles together hosting, accountability, and data-entry responsibility; each participant silently defaults to the model normal in their own system.

turns.inner_thought: I need this settled before the next intake wave or the rollout will generate unnecessary admin for my team. Families liked the pilot because it felt simple and they didn't have to keep repeating themselves. For me, the shared plan is the family-facing PDF summary from our case record, the monthly update needs to be exceptions-based rather than a full standing return, and if the key worker team owns the tracker that means one controlled point of entry on our side.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time, Amir. With the pilot now moving into borough-wide delivery, I'd really like us to come out of today with the practical handoffs nailed down before referrals pick up again. The main things from my end are referral flow into the pathway, what sits in the shared plan, how we handle the monthly update, and making sure the key worker team owns the central tracker so there's one clear home for the cross-agency picture.

turns.inner_thought: That all sounds reasonable. My main concern is that the expanded service still fits NHS governance expectations and doesn't become too informal to support proper oversight. If children can move into the active caseload cleanly and coordinated actions remain visible through the review cycle, I can brief paediatrics and therapies with confidence. When she says the key worker team owns the tracker, I assume they will host and steward it while others contribute updates in the normal way.
turns.utterance: Yes, absolutely. From the health side we're comfortable with the expansion, provided children can move into the active caseload cleanly and partner services can still track coordinated actions properly through the review cycle. If we can get those mechanics straight now, it'll make the brief-out to paediatrics, therapies, and school nursing much easier.

turns.inner_thought: I want children treated as active as soon as a named key worker is allocated and the family accepts support. That's when practical coordination starts, and waiting beyond that just creates an artificial lag in workload and reporting. I'll keep the language broad so it lands as common sense.
turns.utterance: Exactly. My preference is that we move referrals into the active caseload quickly, so once they're in the pathway the named key worker can start coordinating straight away rather than everyone waiting for the process to catch up. That should also keep our routine numbers closer to what's actually being held.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine as stated. In my head, the case becomes truly live across services once the first documented multi-agency review has happened and the coordinated plan is formally open. After that, those active cases can feed into standard health reporting without a separate conversion step.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think that's workable. If we move referrals into the active caseload quickly, then after the first review those active cases can feed straight into the health side's regular reporting without us having to build some separate extra step.

turns.inner_thought: Now I need to anchor the document content without inviting a separate parallel system. The shared plan, as I mean it, is the PDF summary families can actually use, and it should just carry the essentials: actions, owners, deadlines, family priorities.
turns.utterance: On the documentation side, I'd keep it pretty straightforward. The shared plan should show current actions, owners, deadlines, and the latest family priorities before the next review cycle, so everyone is working from the same picture.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'm thinking of the structured MDT template in the Teams workspace, with standard sections populated by participating services around the review. I need enough structure that health actions aren't lost in a narrative summary. I'll talk about inputs rather than sections so it doesn't sound too technical.
turns.utterance: I agree. And if therapists and school nursing can provide their inputs for the shared plan ahead of the review, the meeting itself should run much more efficiently because we won't be trying to pull everything together in real time.

turns.inner_thought: This is the point where I need to protect the service from becoming a reporting hub. 'Current action statuses' should mean changes, slippage, escalation, anything meaningful since last month—not a line-by-line restatement of every open action.
turns.utterance: In terms of the monthly update, I'd like that to stay proportionate. It should include current action statuses so partners can see what is still open and what has moved on, but with the emphasis on anything that's changed, slipped, or needs attention since the previous month.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds acceptable. For me, 'current action statuses' means the standing position across every active child and every open action each month, including items with no change. I can treat her 'proportionate' comment as meaning a clean format rather than a narrower dataset.
turns.utterance: That sounds workable from our side. Having current action statuses each month will help health and therapy leads see what is still open and what has moved on across the active children, and it should give us a reliable view of the standing position.

turns.inner_thought: Now the tracker. I need clear central control so families aren't repeating themselves and we don't end up with multiple agencies editing live entries in different ways. Ownership, to me, means my team maintains the record and partners send amendments in.
turns.utterance: The other piece I'd like to pin down is the tracker. I think the key worker team should own the central tracker so there's one clear home for cross-agency actions, and so families aren't being asked for the same update in three different places.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, that's the right arrangement. In my mind, ownership means they host it, keep the conventions straight, and make sure people contribute on time, while agencies ensure their updates are entered promptly. I'll keep this phrased broadly so it stays aligned.
turns.utterance: Yes, agreed. If the key worker team owns it, we should be able to make sure our updates are reflected promptly after reviews, which ought to help with timeliness and cut down the chasing later on.

turns.inner_thought: Good, this sounds aligned. I'll give a light recap without over-specifying anything: active list quickly, shared plan with the essentials, monthly status visibility, tracker owned by us. That should leave enough room to run this simply on our side.
turns.utterance: That's helpful. I think we're basically there then: referrals move into the active list quickly, the shared plan carries the core actions and family priorities, we give partners a monthly view of current action statuses, and the tracker sits with the key worker team as the central place for the cross-agency picture.

turns.inner_thought: That matches my understanding well enough. I'll brief paediatrics and therapy leads on the basis that the process is now settled: active cases feeding through the review cycle, the shared plan as the working cross-agency document, monthly status reporting, and the tracker owned centrally with health updates visible there.
turns.utterance: Yes, that matches my understanding. I'll brief the paediatrics and therapy leads that we're aligned for the next cycle and that they can rely on the shared plan, the monthly status update, and the tracker arrangement as agreed.
